The Section on Detailed Exposition (Paṭiniddesavāra) – Analysis 3
The Analysis of the Mode of Conveying Logical Connections (Yuttihāravibhaṅga).
Therein, what is the mode of conveying logical connections?
“Of all the modes [of conveying]”—this is the mode of conveying logical connections.
What does it apply?
The four great authorities: the authority of the Buddha, the authority of the Saṅgha, the authority of many elders, and the authority of a single elder.
These four great authorities—those words and phrases—should be brought down into the Sutta, shown to be in accordance with the Vinaya, and set alongside the nature of phenomena (dhammatā).
In which discourse should they be applied?
In the four noble truths.
In which discipline should they be demonstrated?
In the subduing of lust, the subduing of hatred, and the subduing of delusion—
upon what natural law should these be placed?
Upon dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda).

If it enters into the four noble truths, is seen to conform to the discipline for the subduing of the defilements, and does not contradict the true nature of phenomena (*dhammatā*), then it does not generate taints (*āsava*).
Whatever accords with the four great authorities (*mahāpadesa*)—in whatever way it accords and however it accords—that should be accepted.
By one who asks a question, how many terms does he ask about? He should thoroughly investigate and discern [the teaching] term by term.
If all the phrases express a single meaning, that is one question.
Or if four phrases express a single meaning, that is one question.
Or if three phrases express a single meaning, that is one question.
Now, when two phrases express one meaning, that is one question.
When one phrase expresses one meaning, that is another question.
Examining this, it should be understood: "Are these states different in meaning and different in phrasing, or do these states have one meaning and only the phrasing is different?"
How might it be? Just as that deity asks the Blessed One a question:
"By what is the world buffeted?"
By what is he surrounded?
By what dart has he been pierced?
By what is he constantly consumed by smoke?
These four phrases have been asked.
How are those three questions understood?
For the Blessed One answers them for the deity.
“The world is struck down by death,
surrounded by old age,
and pierced by the dart of craving.”
“Always fumigated by desire.
In this context, aging and death are these two conditioned characteristics of the conditioned.
The alteration of that which stands in aging is decay; death is passing away.
In this context, there is a difference in meaning between aging and death.
For what reason? Because even those in the womb die, yet they do not become aged;
and while gods experience death, their bodies do not age.
It is indeed possible to provide a remedy for aging, but it is not possible to provide a remedy for death, except within the domain of those possessing supernormal powers (*iddhi*).
As for the statement that "one is pierced by the arrow of craving," we see those free from lust (*vītarāga*) both growing old and dying.
And if craving were like aging and death [in being unavoidable], [it would likewise be seen in those free from lust].
If that were so, all those in the prime of youth would be free from craving.

And just as craving is the origin of suffering, so too would aging and death be the origin of suffering, and craving would not be the origin of suffering; for aging and death are not the origin of suffering—it is craving that is the origin of suffering.
And just as craving is to be abandoned by the path, so too would aging and death be to be abandoned by the path.
By this method of reasoning, one should investigate through various causes.
And if it appears consistent, even if there is a difference in meaning, it should be investigated even from the perspective of the phrasing.
For instance, "a dart" (*salla*) and "smoking" (*dhūpāyana*): these phenomena are identical in meaning.
For it is not logical that desire (*icchā*) and craving (*taṇhā*) should be different in meaning.
When the intention of craving is not fulfilled, anger (*kodha*) and resentment (*upanāha*) arise toward the nine grounds for malice.
By this reasoning, aging (*jarā*), death (*maraṇa*), and craving (*taṇhā*) are different in meaning.
Furthermore, that which has been described by the Blessed One under two names— namely, "desire" (icchā) and "craving" (taṇhā)— has been described by the Blessed One under these two names,
"desire" and "craving," by way of external objects as its objective support;
for all craving has a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of clinging.
Just as all fire has a single characteristic by way of the characteristic of heat, yet receives various names according to its fuel—
such as "wood-fire," "grass-fire," "splinter-fire," "cow-dung-fire," "chaff-fire," or "rubbish-fire"—
for all fire indeed possesses only the characteristic of heat.
Thus, all craving has a single characteristic by way of the characteristic of attachment;
nevertheless, according to its grasping of objects, it is designated by various names:
it is called "longing," "craving," "muddiness," "fuming," "streaming," "clinging," "affection," "fatigue," "creeper," "conceit," "bondage," "expectation," and "thirst."
“Delight” (*abhinandanā*)—thus, all craving has a single characteristic by way of the characteristic of clinging (*ajjhosāna*).
And as it was stated in the synonyms:
“Hope, longing, and delight.”
“The streams that have settled in many elements,
yearned for and originating from the root of ignorance—
all of them, together with their roots, have been brought to an end by me.”
This is a synonym for craving (taṇhā).
As the Blessed One said:
"Tissa, for one who is not free from lust for form, not free from desire, not free from affection, not free from thirst, and not free from fever."

In the same way, for one who has not become free from lust, desire, affection, thirst, and fever for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, the entire sutta should be expanded in detail.
This is a synonym for craving (*taṇhā*), and thus it is appropriate.

All approaches to suffering have their root in sensual craving and mental formations; however, it is not appropriate [to say] that all approaches to disenchantment have their root in the equipment of sensual craving.
By this method, one should investigate through various reasons. For instance,
the Blessed One teaches foulness (*asubha*) to a person of lustful temperament (*rāgacarita*), he teaches loving-kindness (*mettā*) to a person of hateful temperament (*dosacarita*),
and he teaches dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) to a person of deluded temperament (*mohacarita*).
For if the Blessed One were to teach the liberation of mind through loving-kindness (*mettā-cetovimutti*) to a person of lustful temperament;

or if he were to teach the pleasant practice with sluggish direct knowledge, or the pleasant practice with swift direct knowledge, or abandonment preceded by insight—such a teaching would not be appropriate.
This applies to whatever is a suitable abandonment for lust, a suitable abandonment for hatred, or a suitable abandonment for delusion.
Having investigated all that by means of the method of investigation, it should be applied by means of the method of application.
To whatever extent there is a domain for knowledge:
for one who dwells in loving-kindness, the teaching that "ill-will will persist, having overwhelmed the mind" is untenable; the teaching that "ill-will is abandoned and comes to an end" is tenable.
For one who dwells in compassion, it is not tenable as a teaching that cruelty should persist by obsessing the mind; it is tenable as a teaching that cruelty is abandoned and comes to an end.
For one who dwells in sympathetic joy, it is not tenable as a teaching that aversion should persist by obsessing the mind; it is tenable as a teaching that aversion is abandoned and comes to an end.
For one who dwells in equanimity, it is not tenable as a teaching that lust should persist by obsessing the mind; it is tenable as a teaching that lust is abandoned and comes to an end.

For one who dwells in the signless, it is not logical to teach that consciousness proceeds by following signs here and there; rather, it is logical to teach that the sign is abandoned and passes away.
"The thought 'I am' has vanished; I do not perceive 'this I am.
Yet, 'What am I? and 'How am I?'—such doubt and the arrow of perplexity still obsess my mind."
The teaching that "he will remain" is not tenable; the teaching that "doubt and the arrow of perplexity are abandoned and come to an end" is tenable.
Or again, for one who has attained the first jhāna, the teaching that sensual desire and ill-will lead to distinction is not tenable; the teaching that they lead to decline is tenable.
Or, the teaching that perceptions and mental orientations accompanied by applied thought lead to distinction is not tenable; the teaching that they lead to decline is tenable.

For one who has attained the second jhāna, it is not tenable as a teaching to say that perceptions and mental attentions accompanied by applied and sustained thought lead to distinction; rather, it is tenable as a teaching to say they lead to decline.

Or, it is not tenable as a teaching to say that perceptions and mental attentions accompanied by equanimity and bliss lead to decline; rather, it is tenable as a teaching to say they lead to distinction.
For one who has attained the third jhāna, [it is not tenable] that perceptions and mental attentions accompanied by rapture and bliss lead to distinction... [as before].
The teaching that "perceptions and acts of attention accompanied by equanimity and purity of mindfulness lead to decline" is not tenable; the teaching that they "lead to distinction" is tenable.

For one who has attained the fourth jhāna, the teaching that "perceptions and acts of attention accompanied by equanimity lead to distinction" is not tenable; the teaching that they "lead to decline" is tenable.
It is not tenable to teach that perception and attention associated with the base of infinite space lead to decline; it is tenable to teach that they lead to distinction.

It is not tenable to teach that for one who has attained the base of infinite space, perception and attention associated with form lead to distinction; it is tenable to teach that they lead to decline.
It is not tenable to teach that perception and attention associated with the base of infinite consciousness lead to decline; it is tenable to teach that they lead to distinction.

For one who has attained the base of infinite consciousness, it is not tenable as a teaching to say that perceptions and mental orientations associated with the base of infinite space lead to distinction; rather, it is tenable as a teaching to say they lead to decline.

Or, for one [in that state], it is not tenable as a teaching to say that perceptions and mental orientations associated with the base of nothingness lead to decline; rather, it is tenable as a teaching to say they lead to distinction.

For one who has attained the base of nothingness, it is not tenable as a teaching to say that perceptions and mental orientations associated with the base of infinite consciousness lead to distinction; rather, it is tenable as a teaching to say they lead to decline.

Or, for one [attained to the base of nothingness], it is not tenable as a teaching to say that perceptions and mental orientations associated with the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception lead to decline; rather, it is tenable as a teaching to say they lead to distinction.

For one who has attained the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the teaching that "perceptions and mental applications lead to distinction" is not tenable; the teaching that they "lead to decline" is tenable.

The teaching that "perceptions and mental applications associated with the cessation of perception and feeling lead to decline" is not tenable; the teaching that they "lead to distinction" is tenable.

The teaching that "a mind accustomed to pliancy does not tolerate an exertion [of will]" is not tenable; the teaching that "a mind accustomed to pliancy nevertheless tolerates an exertion [of will]" is tenable.

Thus, all nine types of suttas, having been investigated in every way by means of the method of investigation according to the Dhamma, according to the Vinaya, and according to the Teacher’s instruction, should be applied by means of the method of application.
Therefore the Venerable Mahākaccāyana said: “Whatever is the ground and whatever is the range of all the methods.
The method of application is concluded.
